content.p: For most of a week in January 1923, white men from Sumner and surrounding towns hunted through the Black settlement of Rosewood in Levy County. They were looking for a man a white woman said had attacked her. When they were done, the community was gone. The official count was eight dead, six Black residents and two white men, but some later accounts reckon the toll much higher. Survivors had hidden in cold swamps and then scattered, and the town was abandoned.

No one was charged with any killing or any fire. A grand jury met within weeks and found nothing on which to base an indictment. The silence that followed lasted close to sixty years, until a newspaper reporter went looking. In 1994 the Florida Legislature, after hearings in which survivors testified, voted compensation. Some sources describe it as the only government reparations ever paid in the United States to victims of anti-Black racial violence.
content.h2: A small town and a violent region
content.p: Rosewood was surveyed in 1847 and became a village around 1870, when a railroad station was built, according to EBSCO's research summary. By 1900 it was a mostly Black community with Black-owned businesses, churches and schools. Its size depends on who is counting. CNN gives about 200 residents, while a slide presentation by Martha Barnett, a lawyer for the survivors, says about 120. The historian Maxine D. Jones, writing in the Florida Historical Quarterly, cites a Black population of 342 for the whole precinct in the 1920 census and puts the number of families in Rosewood proper at eighteen to twenty-five, most of them owning their homes and land.

Jones describes Emma and James Carrier's two-story house with glass windows, two porches and an organ, and the home of Sarah and Heyward Carrier, which had a piano. Residents hunted and farmed, and Emma Carrier sold eggs and vegetables from her garden. Some worked in Sumner, three miles to the west: the men at the Cummer Lumber Mill, the women in white households. Remembering Rosewood says the only white family in town were the Wrights, who ran the last store.

Levy County had recorded one lynching, in 1904, but Jones points out that its neighbours had a worse record. She counts at least sixteen Black people lynched in Alachua County between 1900 and 1922, and Florida led the country in lynchings in 1920 with eleven. Barnett's timeline adds the Election Day killings at Ocoee in November 1920, the burning of a Black church, school and lodge at Perry in December, less than a month before Rosewood, after a white teacher was murdered there, and a large Ku Klux Klan parade in Gainesville on New Year's Eve 1922.

On the morning of Monday 1 January 1923, Fannie Taylor of Sumner, a married white woman whose husband was at work at the sawmill, said she had been attacked by a Black man. Some accounts say she was also raped. A posse formed, and the search centred on Jesse Hunter, described as an escaped convict. Libcom's short history says he was blamed on no better evidence than that.

The accusation was disputed from the start. EBSCO reports a later claim that the assault was committed by a white man with whom Taylor had been having an affair. Jones is more specific. Sarah Carrier, a Rosewood matriarch, was working for Taylor that morning and disputed her account; Jones writes that the man Carrier and her eleven-year-old granddaughter Philomena Goins saw leaving the house was white. With Taylor white and Carrier Black, Jones comments, Carrier's word counted for little.

Bloodhounds led the posse to the home of Aaron Carrier on the edge of Rosewood. The men accused him of helping Hunter and seized him. Sheriff Elias Walker intervened and, according to EBSCO, took him into protective custody. Remembering Rosewood tells it more harshly: Carrier was dragged behind a car and left for dead. In the afternoon the posse caught Sam Carter, a 45-year-old blacksmith, whom the mob believed had used his wagon to carry the fugitive away. EBSCO says Carter was tortured, shot and lynched. Barnett's slides quote Ernest Parham, a 19-year-old white man who came on the scene: "When I caught up with the group, they had him strung up on a tree there." Parham said Carter was let down, took them to the place where he thought he had put the man out, and was shot when the dogs picked up no trail. The slides add that a coroner's inquest later found Carter had been killed by an "unknown party".
content.h2: Thursday night at the Carrier house
content.p: Armed white men began gathering in Sumner on 2 January, and Barnett's slides say Ku Klux Klan members returning from the Gainesville parade were probably among them. The rumor was that Aaron's cousin Sylvester Carrier was sheltering Hunter. EBSCO adds that he was said to be openly supporting the alleged attack on Taylor.

Jones says Sylvester, believing there was safety in numbers, persuaded his relatives to gather in his parents' two-story house. Relatives from two households came: James and Emma Carrier with their children and grandchildren, Sarah's own children and grandchildren, and Sylvester's wife Gertrude. On the evening of Thursday 4 January a group of white men came to the house. BlackPast puts them at twenty to thirty and says they shot the family dog. When the people inside refused to come out, Jones writes, the men started shooting, and Sylvester Carrier returned fire for several hours. EBSCO says it is unclear who fired first.

Sarah Carrier was killed. The survivor Minnie Lee Langley testified that she was shot through a window, while BlackPast says she was shot on the porch. Sylvester was killed too. Two of the attackers, Poly Wilkerson and Henry Andrews, died, and BlackPast says four more men were wounded. Among those hurt inside were Reubin Mitchell, who lost an eye, and Emma Carrier, shot in the hand and wrist. Langley was nine years old. She told legislators in 1994 that Sylvester hid her in a wood bin beneath the stairs and fired over her shoulder when Wilkerson kicked in the door. Those still alive fled to the swamp in their night clothes, and Jones notes that the new year had brought unusually cold weather.

BlackPast says that the next day a crowd of about 200 men from surrounding towns joined the mob, having heard wrongly that a Black man had killed two white men. Barnett's slides put the arrivals on 5 January at 200 to 300. Remembering Rosewood says men from neighboring counties, including Ku Klux Klan members, swelled the numbers. Barnett says the governor, Cary Hardee, was notified on 5 January and that Sheriff Walker reported he feared "no further disorder".

The accounts do not agree on exactly when each death occurred. Jones says that when the white men returned on Friday to collect their dead, they burned the Carrier house and five more houses and a Black church, and that Lexie Gordon, a widow in her mid-fifties, was shot when she came out from under her burning home. Mingo Williams was killed near Bronson. Jones places James Carrier's death on Saturday 6 January: he had suffered two strokes, and twenty-five or thirty white men took him to the Black cemetery, questioned him and, reputedly, made him dig his own grave before shooting him. Barnett's timeline puts the Gordon killing on 4 January and the Carrier killing on 5 January. Both versions give the same six Black victims: Sam Carter, Sarah Carrier, Sylvester Carrier, Lexie Gordon, Mingo Williams and James Carrier.

Sunday 7 January was the last day. Jones says white men burned the remaining twelve or thirteen buildings, and Barnett puts the mob at 100 to 150. The only building left was the home of John Wright, the white storekeeper. A 1923 newspaper account quoted by Jones described twisted steel from the furniture and charred bodies of dogs among the ruins.

Langley remembered spending at least two nights in the swamps, and Jones says concerned white people arranged a train to take the women and children to safety. BlackPast credits two train conductors, John and William Bryce, with evacuating people on 6 January, and says John Wright hid others. The survivors went to Gainesville and then on to other Florida towns and northern cities. According to Barnett, many settled in Lacoochee, in Pasco County.

Jones follows several families afterwards. Langley's grandmother Emma, wounded in the shootout, died in 1924, and Langley went on to work for decades in Jacksonville, never telling her husband or daughter what she had lived through. Philomena Goins later sang with a band and shared a stage with Ella Fitzgerald, but Jones writes that she never trusted white people again.

The figure most often repeated is eight, six Black residents and two white men, and Barnett's slides call it the official toll. EBSCO says the lack of records and of reliable press reporting makes the true extent hard to know, and that the number of Black dead was at least six but possibly as many as forty. Libcom's short history says the death toll is assumed to be nearer 27. Remembering Rosewood adds that no one can account for any deaths during the frantic escape.

A grand jury convened on 11 February 1923, according to Barnett's timeline, and on 15 February found insufficient evidence to prosecute. Barnett also says no state or local law enforcement official ever investigated the killings, and the SPLC says the same of any law enforcement agency. No arrest for murder or arson was made, according to EBSCO, and Jesse Hunter's capture was never confirmed. EBSCO adds that survivors, out of fear, chose not to speak.

In July 1982 Gary Moore of the St. Petersburg Times published his findings. EBSCO says he had noticed that history texts described Black residents in communities near Rosewood that were almost entirely white decades later. He found survivors and witnesses. CBS aired a 60 Minutes report in December 1983, and Barnett's slides say survivors began speaking out.

The Florida law firm Holland and Knight met Minnie Lee Langley in 1992, Barnett says, and she and Ruth Davis became its first clients. Arnett Doctor then helped identify other survivors. EBSCO says the survivors led by Doctor were inspired by the reparations paid to Japanese Americans interned in the Second World War.

The Legislature commissioned a study. Five historians, Jones, David Colburn, R. Thomas Dye, Larry Rivers and William Rogers, gave the Board of Regents their report on 22 December 1993, under the title A Documented History of the Incident Which Occurred at Rosewood. EBSCO says it drew on contemporary news reports and interviews with survivors.

The lawyers chose the Legislature over the courts. Barnett says the records were incomplete or missing and that limitation periods were a legal obstacle. House and Senate claim bills were filed on 4 January 1994, seventy-one years after the violence began, sponsored by Representatives Miguel De Grandy and Al Lawson and Senator Darrell Jones. They sought $7.2 million. The SPLC says the descendants lobbied conservative lawmakers by stressing property rights rather than racial justice, and overcame fears among Black legislators that the issue was too divisive. Barnett quotes one description of the measure as "the most controversial claim bill ever considered by the Florida Legislature".

A special master heard testimony from 4 to 18 March. Barnett says the survivors Arnett Goins, then 79, and Minnie Lee Langley, then 80, described being hidden upstairs in the Carrier house as children, seeing the bodies of the white men, and fleeing into the swamp in their night clothes. Her case, she says, rested not on the mob but on the officials who did nothing to stop it. According to her slides the state admitted the facts were true and also argued that there was no legal basis for the claims, which it said were barred by the statute of limitations.

The special master's report, filed on 30 March, concluded that the state had a moral obligation. It recommended $150,000 for each elderly survivor, a fund for property losses and a university scholarship fund for descendants, and that police conduct a complete investigation to see whether any prosecution was still possible. House Bill 591 mirrored those recommendations, Barnett says. It passed on 9 April and Governor Lawton Chiles signed it on 4 May 1994. Libcom gives the signing date as 23 May.

The bill's text, quoted by CNN, said local and state officials knew of the conflict, had time and opportunity to act, and failed to prevent the destruction of the town. It said authorities failed to investigate properly, to bring the perpetrators to justice and to secure the area for residents to return safely. The total was $2.1 million, according to the SPLC. EBSCO says $500,000 of it was for descendants of residents whose property was destroyed and the rest formed a pool for scholarships. BlackPast says nine survivors were entitled to $150,000 each. Libcom says 172 people received money. These accounts differ.

Four years later, the SPLC reports, Florida allowed descendants of Rosewood victims to attend state colleges and universities tuition-free, and more than 300 have done so. CNN cites a 2020 Washington Post report of at least 297 recipients of the scholarship. John Singleton's film Rosewood appeared in 1997. In 2004 Governor Jeb Bush travelled to the site to dedicate a Florida Heritage Landmark marker, which, according to the SPLC, memorialises those who died.

For the centennial in January 2023, the SPLC reported, descendants and others planned a week of events, including a wreath-laying at the site and gatherings at the University of Florida law school in Gainesville. A historian, in remarks published in 2023, places Rosewood among comparable attacks on Black communities, at Wilmington in 1898, Elaine in 1919, Tulsa in 1921 and Ocoee in 1920, and notes that in Florida a lynching at Newberry came in 1916 and killings at Perry less than a month before Rosewood.
